## Paper

## Abstract

The manufacture of nitriles is critical to various industrial applications, but poor selectivity results in the significant release of pollutive byproducts such as CO , NO and toxic cyanide. Here, we report the electrochemical conversion of benzaldehyde to benzonitrile at near-unity selectivity, during which Co O clusters-decorated Cu O electrocatalyst activates the C−N bond of an unstable intermediate species. Operando spectroelectrochemical studies and theoretical calculations reveal that benzaldehyde couples with NH to form the phenylmethanimine intermediate bound atop Cu2+ active sites, which facilitates hydrogen transfer from the imine group to nearby surface oxygen. Our electrochemical system can convert aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes to the corresponding nitriles at Faradaic efficiencies of 78-97%. This can be paired with cathodic NO reduction, which produces a commensurable amount of NH to that consumed even at a current density of 200 mA cm-2. Our work offers a clean synthetic route to otherwise-pollutive chemicals, and also expands the repertoire of organonitrogen compounds that can be accessed by electrocatalysis.

---

## Introduction

Nitriles have far-ranging applications in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, dyes and polymers1. For example, benzonitrile is manufactured at 10 million kg per year due to its importance as a building block in pharmaceuticals and melamine resins2. Currently, nitriles are manufactured through the ammoxidation of alkanes3,4, alcohols or aldehydes5 with ammonia and oxygen at high temperatures (Fig. 1a). These conditions require heavy energy consumption and result in low selectivity, leading to the release of CO , NO and over-oxidation products6. Other synthesis methods, such as the Sandmeyer reaction and Rosenmund-von Braun reaction, require stoichiometric amounts of toxic cyanide reagents7,8 (Fig. 1b); more than one million tons of cyanide are consumed per year by the chemicals industry9, which generate hazardous wastes due to incomplete cyanide consumption or production of cyanide derivatives10. Thus, it is important to develop cleaner methods of nitriles synthesis that can utilize renewable energy and benign conditions, while avoiding cyanide reagents.

Recently, there has been great interest in electrochemical C−N coupling reactions, as they offer a sustainable route for producing valuable organonitrogen compounds such as urea, amides, amines, oximes and amino acids11-25. Comparatively, nitriles have a higher degree of unsaturation; a different electrochemical route must be designed to access this type of C≡N bond. Previously, it has been reported that copper salt can catalyze the thermal ammoxidation of aldehydes to nitriles; Cu2+ binds to the aldimine intermediate to form an iminylcuprate complex, which then dissociates to Cu+ and the nitrile product26. This led us to consider the possibility of enabling ‘electrochemical ammoxidation’ by building Cuδ+ into our electrocatalyst. We also note that the oxidative nature of the reaction means that it can be coupled to the cathodic nitrogen oxides reduction reaction (NO RR) to NH , which suggests that waste NO in industrial exhaust can be utilized as a N-source to enhance the sustainability of the reaction (Fig. 1c).

In this work, we demonstrate the electrocatalytic conversion of benzaldehyde to benzonitrile using NH as a benign nitrogen source under ambient conditions. This is achieved with an electrocatalyst comprising Co O clusters-decorated Cu O nanorod array (Co OS/Cu O), which enabled Faradaic efficiency of 98.7(±1.1)% and near-unity selectivity under an applied potential of 1.35 V vs. RHE. The electrocatalyst remains stable with Faradaic efficiency averaging 95.4(±2.5)% over 100 hours. Operando spectroelectrochemical and density function theory (DFT) studies show that benzaldehyde couples with NH to form an unstable phenylmethanimine intermediate, which subsequently undergoes Cuδ+-mediated electrochemical dehydrogenation to benzonitrile. The electrochemical benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion can be integrated into reaction pathways that enable the nitrilation of more challenging alcohol and alkyl groups. Our electrochemical system can also convert other aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes, including those derived from CO , to the corresponding nitriles with Faradaic efficiencies of 78-97%. Finally, we demonstrated tandem benzonitrile electrosynthesis and NO RR at current densities up to 200 mA cm-2.

---

## Results

Electrocatalyst design and characterization
We prepared the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst by chemical oxidation of copper foam in an aqueous NaOH and (NH ) S O solution, which embellished the surface with Cu(OH) nanorods, followed by immersion in a solution containing ZIF-67 metal-organic framework and annealing in air at 350°C (see characterization of the Cu(OH) and ZIF-67/Cu(OH) nanorod arrays in Supplementary Figs. 1-2). Co K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy indicated that the ZIF-67 was successfully converted to Co O , as the absorption edge of Co O /Cu O displayed identical features to that of the Co O standard (Supplementary Fig. 3). The Fourier-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra revealed oscillations corresponding to Co−O, the Co−Co bond with octahedral centers, and the Co−Co bond with octahedral and tetrahedral centers, which further confirms the formation of Co O cluster27. High-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) with corresponding EDX mapping showed that the Co O cluster took the form of a slightly concave octahedron attached to the tip of the Cu O nanorod (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 4). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed an array of cluster-on-nanorod morphology on the copper foam surface (Fig. 2b). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern showed peaks at 35.5°, 38.7°, 61.5° corresponding to (11-1), (111) and (11-3) lattice planes of CuO, as well as 36.5° and 61.5° corresponding to (111) and (220) lattice planes of Cu O (Supplementary Fig. 5)28. This is corroborated by high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), which revealed crystalline phases with lattice spacings of 0.242 and 0.234 nm corresponding to Cu O(111) and CuO(111), respectively. It should be noted that both Cu O(110) and Cu O(111) facets were observed (Supplementary Fig. 6), with the dominant one being the (111) surface. The Co O cluster also appeared to be highly crystalline, with lattice spacings of 0.246 and 0.287 nm corresponding to (311) and (220) planes (Fig. 2c).

Electrochemical conversion of benzaldehyde to benzonitrile
The electrochemical C−N coupling of benzaldehyde and ammonia to benzonitrile was conducted in a three-electrode H-type cell, with a working electrode comprising Co O /Cu O on copper foam, an Ag/AgCl reference electrode and a platinum plate counter electrode (Supplementary Fig. 7). The optimal anolyte concentration comprised 0.04 M benzaldehyde, 2.0 M NH and 0.1 M NaOH in a 41:9 water:acetonitrile mixture (Supplementary Fig. 8-9). The catholyte is an aqueous 0.1 M NaOH solution, and is separated from the anolyte by Nafion® 117 membrane. The Faradaic efficiencies towards benzonitrile showed a volcano-type tendency in the potential range of 1.15-1.65 V vs. RHE, with the optimal Faradaic efficiency at 98.7(±1.1)% at 1.35 V vs. RHE (Fig. 2d). Beyond 1.55 V vs. RHE, the Faradaic efficiency decreases significantly due to competing NH oxidation reaction. This is corroborated by the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curve, which revealed the NH oxidation peak to be about 1.5 V vs. RHE under reaction conditions (Supplementary Fig. 10). The yield of benzonitrile reached 48.6(±6.7)% after 1 hour of reaction at 1.55 V vs. RHE, and further increased to 75.0(±1.5)% after 3 hours (Supplementary Fig. 11). The selectivity towards benzonitrile was ~100% with no obvious byproducts detected (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Figs. 12-13). No benzonitrile was detected at open-circuit voltage (OCV), without applied potential or in the absence of NH , which confirms the electrochemical nature of the reaction and the important role of NH as the nitrogen source (Supplementary Fig. 14).

We investigated the robustness of the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst by subjecting it to a constant potential of 1.35 V vs. RHE for 100 hours, during which portions of the electrolyte were periodically removed for analysis and replaced with fresh electrolyte. Under these conditions, the electrocatalyst achieved a stable current density of ~10 mA cm-2, with an average Faradaic efficiency of 95.4(±2.5)% (Fig. 2e). Post-reaction characterizations of the electrocatalyst (i.e., SEM, EDX, XANES, EXAFS and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), see Supplementary Figs. 15-18) showed no obvious change in the structure or composition, which suggests its compatibility for long-term operation.

Investigation of reaction mechanism
Having established the efficacy of Co O /Cu O towards benzonitrile production, we studied the role of different components in the electrocatalyst. The Cu O electrocatalyst without Co O clusters was also prepared (see characterization in Supplementary Figs. 19-20) and yielded a Faradaic efficiency of 71.8(±3.1)% at 1.35 V vs. RHE, which suggests that Cu O functions as the main catalytic component driving the benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion (Supplementary Fig. 21). Only trace benzonitrile product was detected when pristine copper foam (CF) was used as the working electrode (Supplementary Fig. 22), which suggests that either Cu2+ or Cu+ should function as the electrocatalytic active site in Cu O. We performed operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to study the electrode/electrolyte interface during reaction (Fig. 3a)29. At potentials between 0.5-1.0 V vs. RHE, we observed a signal in the middle-frequency region (100-102 Hz) that corresponds to the electrooxidation of the Cu O catalyst (i.e., Cu0Cu+Cu2+). This is consistent with the cyclic voltammetry (CV) curve, which showed two distinct oxidation peaks at 0.60 and 0.85 V vs. RHE corresponding to Cu0Cu+ and Cu0/Cu+Cu2+, respectively28 (Supplementary Fig. 23). At potentials >1.05 V vs. RHE, the signal is observed in the low-frequency region (10-1-100 Hz), which is related to the appearance of oxidation species on the surface of the electrode. This signifies that the structural evolution of Cuδ+ is complete and the benzaldehyde electrosynthesis occurs. In situ Raman spectroscopy showed distinctive peaks at 218 and 294 cm−1 at OCV, which can be attributed to Cu O and CuO, respectively (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Figs. 24-25). In the absence of benzaldehyde and NH , the Cu O peak disappeared at 1.35 V vs. RHE, indicating the oxidation of Cu+ to Cu2+. With benzaldehyde and NH , the Cu O peak can still be observed at 1.35 V vs. RHE, while the CuO peak showed reduced intensity compared to that at OCV, which suggests that Cu2+ catalyzed the benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion and was reverted to Cu+ in the process.

The reaction mechanism was further probed using in situ attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), by tracking the adsorbed intermediates and products on Cu O/CF at potentials from OCV to 1.65 V vs. RHE (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 26). Under OCV, peaks were observed at 1700, 1371, 1233 and 1138 cm-1, which could be assigned to the C=O stretching vibration of benzaldehyde, alcoholic O−H group, the N−H twisting vibration of CH −NH structure and the NH stretching vibration of CH −NH structure, respectively23,30. This implies that NH , which has a relatively strong nucleophilicity, can spontaneously attack benzaldehyde to form amino(phenyl)methanol, which undergoes dehydration to generate the unstable *benzyl-azane intermediate. As the potential increased to 1.15 V vs. RHE, the NH peak at 1138 cm-1 is diminished while the N−H peak at 1233 cm-1 is slightly enhanced. We observed the emergence of peaks corresponding to the N−H stretching vibration of CH=NH structure at 1296 cm-1, C=N stretching vibration at 1624 cm-1 and C≡N stretching vibration at 2259 cm-1, which indicates the formation of phenylmethanimine intermediate and benzonitrile product23,30. As the potential increases up to 1.65 V vs. RHE, the NH and N−H absorption peaks of unstable amino(phenyl)methanol and *benzyl-azane intermediates are weakened, whereas the C=N bond and C≡N peaks of phenylmethanimine and benzonitrile are generally strengthened. This signified that amino(phenyl)methanol and *benzyl-azane intermediates rapidly converted to the critical phenylmethanimine intermediate, which subsequently could be dehydrogenated to generate the benzonitrile. Liquid chromatography-quadrupole time of flight mass spectrometry (LC-QTOF) also ascertained the presence of phenylmethanimine intermediate and benzonitrile product in the post-reaction anolyte (Fig. 3d). The use of 15N-labelled NH yielded 15N-labelled phenylmethanimine and benzonitrile, which reinforced the important role of NH as a nitrogen source in benzonitrile electrosynthesis (Supplementary Fig. 27). Taken together, we postulate that NH readily undergoes C−N coupling with the carbonyl group of benzaldehyde to form an unstable phenylmethanimine intermediate, which subsequently undergoes Cuδ+-mediated electrochemical dehydrogenation to yield the benzonitrile product (Fig. 3e).

We further investigated the Cuδ+-mediated dehydrogenation step through density functional theory (DFT) calculations. A CuO(111) slab model with four atomic layers was constructed, upon which several initial adsorption geometries were examined. The most stable configuration features the imine nitrogen of phenylmethanimine (Ph−CH=NH) binding to a single two-coordinate Cu atom (Configuration 1 in Supplementary Fig. 28). This geometry suggests a possible adsorption mode in which the =NH moiety is in proximity with the surface, potentially enabling the abstraction of the N-bound hydrogen. Within the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) framework, this hydrogen is removed as a coupled proton–electron pair rather than transferred to or stabilized on any surface atoms31. The resultant molecule adopts an sp3-like configuration and relocates to a bridge site coordinated by two Cu atoms (Supplementary Figs. 29c,d). The hydrogen atom from the CH= moiety is then abstracted by the surface to form the nitrile product (C≡N), culminating in the final state where the nitrogen atom bind s atop a single Cu atom (Supplementary Figs. 29e,f). This second hydrogen transfer is calculated to be thermodynamically more favorable than the first, as reflected by the downhill reaction energy (G). Overall, the G of phenylmethanimine dehydrogenation on CuO(111) is 0.70 eV (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Table 2). In contrast, phenylmethanimine dehydrogenation on Cu O(110) has a higher G of 1.16 eV (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Figs. 30-31), suggesting that Cu2+ species may be more effective for phenylmethanimine dehydrogenation than Cu+ species under the modeled conditions. This is substantiated by Bader charge analysis of the adsorbed phenylmethanimine on CuO(111). As reaction progresses, the phenylmethanimine molecular fragment exhibits an increasingly positive charge; from +0.16 in the initial adsorbed state to +0.85 in the first dehydrogenated intermediate and +2.10 in the final nitrile product (Supplementary Table 3). Correspondingly, CuO(111) exhibits increasingly negative charge (−0.16 → −0.85 → −2.10), which is indicative that the surface Cu2⁺ accepts electrons from phenylmethanimine and is reduced to Cu⁺.

To elucidate the influence of the Co O cluster, we similarly examined the phenylmethanimine dehydrogenation step on the Co O (311) surface (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Figs. 32-33). The calculated G of 0.96 eV lies between those of CuO(111) and Cu O(111), indicating an intermediate oxidizing strength within this computational model. It should be noted that these DFT results are based on idealized static slab models and mainly provide qualitative trends under real catalytic conditions. Experimentally, the Faradaic efficiency of benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion using Co O clusters supported on carbon paper is 32.6(±3.8)% (Supplementary Fig. 34), which suggests that the Co O clusters provide additional active sites that contribute to the enhanced Faradaic efficiency of Co O /Cu O. This is corroborated by the increased double-layer capacitance (C ) of Co O /Cu O compared to Cu O (2.06 versus 1.70 mF cm−2, see Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 35). We also investigated the electronic structure of Co O /Cu O through XPS analysis (Fig. 4b-4c and Supplementary Figs. 36-37). High-resolution Co 2p XPS spectrum showed a negative shift compared to that of pure Co O powder, signifying a lower average Co oxidation state. Cu 2p XPS spectrum of Co O /Cu O showed a higher energy shift compared to that of Cu O, which indicates a higher average Cu oxidation state and suggests electron transfer from Cu to Co within the Co O /Cu O material. The higher average Cu oxidation state promotes the Cuδ+-mediated dehydrogenation step, thereby enabling higher Faradaic efficiencies for electrochemical benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion (Supplementary Fig. 34). Therefore, the decoration of Co O clusters on Cu O electrocatalyst not only increases the active sites, but can potentially modulate the electronic structure of the electrocatalyst, resulting in a higher average Cu oxidation state promoting the Cuδ+-mediated dehydrogenation step.

Electrosynthesis of various nitriles and utilization of NO
The broad applicability of Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst was demonstrated through the electrochemical conversion of various aldehydes to the corresponding nitriles at near-unity selectivities (Supplementary Fig. 38). An application scenario is the electrosynthesis of 2,6-dichlorobenzonitrile, an important herbicide with a market size of $23 million per year32,33; we achieved Faradaic efficiency of 81.2(±1.7)% at 1.35 V vs. RHE. The presence of electron-withdrawing groups such as −Cl, −Br and −CN generally led to higher Faradaic efficiencies of 93-97%, as the enhanced electrophilicity of these benzaldehydes promotes C−N coupling with nucleophilic NH . For electron-donating −CH and −OCH groups, Faradaic efficiencies were lower at 84.2(±6.1) and 77.8(±2.5)%. The Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst can be extended to the electrosynthesis of aliphatic nitriles, such as acetonitrile with a Faradaic efficiency of 86.2(±4.7)%. It should be noted that the acetaldehyde precursor can be obtained from electrochemical CO reduction reaction, thereby enabling the electrosynthesis of nitriles from renewable sources34. We also demonstrated that nitrile electrosynthesis can be integrated into reaction pathways starting from precursors with alcohol and even alkyl groups (Fig. 4d). For example, the electrochemical benzyl alcohol-to-benzonitrile conversion can be achieved Faradaic efficiency at 43.1(±2.0)% (Supplementary Fig. 39). The electrochemical toluene-to-benzonitrile conversion was conducted in two stages; toluene was first oxidized at 100 mA cm-2 for 2 h using a CoO /IrO on Ti mesh electrode to activate the C(sp3)−H bond and achieve sufficient benzaldehyde intermediate, after which NH was added and the reaction continued at 25 mA cm-2 to enable benzonitrile using the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst (Supplementary Fig. 40).

Finally, we considered that the electrochemical valorization of waste NO to nitrogenous chemicals can mitigate pollution and reduce dependence on valuable NH as a nitrogen source. We therefore coupled cathodic NO RR with anodic benzonitrile electrosynthesis in a single electrochemical cell, with the former acting as a NH supply for the latter. Notably, the NH consumption at anode was comparable to NH production at cathode even at current densities up to 200 mA cm-2, which signifies that waste NO can be viably incorporated into valuable nitriles (Figure 4e, Faradaic efficiencies can be found in Supplementary Fig. 43). This also means that the achieved partial current densities and production rates are competitive with other reported nitrile electrosynthesis, while maintaining near-unity selectivity (Supplementary Table 4).

Synthesis and characterization of the Co O /Cu O nanorod array electrocatalyst
The Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst was synthesized by the modified chemical oxidation followed by annealing procedure. Cu foam was ultrasonically cleaned in 3 M HCl solution for 10 min, then in a mixture of acetone and deionized water for another 10 min. The pretreated Cu foam was soaked into a 40 mL aqueous solution containing 4 g NaOH and 1.5 g (NH ) S O for 1 h, then washed with deionized water and ethanol. The resultant Cu(OH) nanorod array was prepared after drying at 60°C. Cu(OH) was immersed into 2 mmol cobaltous nitrate hexahydrate in methanol solution for 10 min, after which 8 mmol 2-methylimidazole in methanol solution was added under stirring and allowed to stand for 6 h. The resultant ZIF-67/Cu(OH) was taken out, washed with deionized water and methanol, dried at 60°C, then annealed at 350°C for 3 h, 2°C min-1 to form the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst.

Electrocatalyst characterization
To characterize the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst, X-ray diffraction (XRD) was detected on Bruker® D8 ADVANCE with Cu Kα source. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were obtained on a Hitachi SU8220 FESEM at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. Energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy was collected with an on-board AMTEK® Octane Elite EDS System, with an accelerating voltage of 20 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were obtained on TEM JEOL 2100F. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was measured on a PHI Quantum 2000 XPS system. X-Ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was conducted on XAFCA beamline at the Singapore Synchrotron Light Source (SSLS).

Evaluation of electrochemical performance
The electrochemical benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversions were conducted in H-type electrolytic cell (purchased from Tianjin Aida). The electrolyte was prepared individually before each experimental run. The anolyte comprised 0.04 M benzaldehyde, 2.0 M NH and 0.1 M NaOH in 41:9 water:acetonitrile mixture (pH=13.16(±0.07)). The catholyte was 0.1 M aqueous NaOH catholyte. Electrochemical double-layer capacitance (C ) measurement was carried out by CV method with different scan rates in the non-Faradaic region. The C value was obtained from the slopes of the current density–scan rate plots. where N is the number of electron transfer to generated product, F is the Faraday constant (96485 C mol−1), C is the concentration of liquid products after the electrosynthesis reaction, V is the volume of the electrolyte, Q is the total charge during the electrosynthesis process, S is the electrode area, t is the electrolysis time, n is the mole amount of consumed feedstock, n is the mole amount of initial feedstock.

Operando spectroelectrochemical studies
In situ ATR-SEIRAS was conducted using PerkinElmer Frontier FT-IR spectrometer equipped with a mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector. The measurements were carried out in a commercial electrochemical cell containing benzaldehyde and NH in 0.1 M aqueous NaOH electrolyte. The electrode was Cu O electrocatalyst on an Au film chemically deposited on the reflecting plane of the ATR Si prism. The background spectrum without applied potential was acquired at electrolyte condition before each systemic measurement. In situ Raman spectra were recorded using a Horiba LabRam Odyssey Nano Raman Spectrometer system with 633 nm laser. The Raman cell was equipped with a working electrode comprising Cu O deposited on carbon paper, an Ag/AgCl reference electrode and a Pt wire counter electrode. The cell was filled with benzaldehyde and NH in 0.1 M NaOH electrolyte. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations
All periodic slab calculations were carried out using density functional theory (DFT) as implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)35. The Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE)36 exchange-correlation functional within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) was employed, along with projector-augmented wave (PAW)37 potentials and a plane-wave energy cutoff of 500 eV. Dispersion interactions were accounted for using the DFT-D3 method38.

Slab models of CuO(111) and Cu O(111) and Co O (311) surfaces were constructed with four atomic layers, where the bottom three layers were fixed during structural optimizations. The CuO(111) slab has lattice parameters a = 17.30 Å, b = 18.95 Å, and c = 28.26 Å, with interaxial angles α = β = 90° and γ = 107.76°. The Cu O(111) surface adopts a = 18.12 Å, b = 18.12 Å, and c = 31.10 Å, with α = β = 90° and γ = 120.00°. The Co O (311) slab exhibits a = 19.85 Å, b = 22.93 Å, and c = 26.31 Å, with α = β = 90° and γ = 106.78°. In all models, the c-axis is oriented normal to the surface plane, and a vacuum region of approximately 20 Å was added along this direction to prevent spurious interactions between periodic images. Brillouin zone sampling was performed using a Γ-centered 1 × 1 × 1 k-point mesh for all adsorption geometry optimizations39. Structural relaxations were conducted until the forces on each atom were below 0.02 eV/Å and the total energy change between successive steps was less than 10-5 eV. To account for the on-site Coulomb interactions in the localized 3d orbitals, the DFT+U method40 was applied with U = 7.0 eV for Cu in CuO41 and U = 4.0 eV for Co in Co O 42.

To rigorously assess the influence of k-point sampling for slabs of this size, we performed a convergence test on the Cu O model (Supplementary Table 1). Increasing the k-point mesh from 1×1×1 to 2×2×1 resulted in only marginal variations (≤0.01 eV) in the computed energy profiles, thereby confirming that Γ-point sampling is sufficient for this lateral cell dimension. On this basis, and given the nearly identical cell sizes across all three systems, the Γ-point (1×1×1) mesh validated for Cu O was consistently used for the CuO and Co O slabs in all subsequent calculations.

For all surfaces, only coordinatively unsaturated (CUS) metal sites were considered as potential adsorption sites. Guided by the surface symmetry and the locations of coordinatively unsaturated sites, we evaluated three, two, and three distinct adsorption geometries on the CuO(111), Cu O(111) and Co O (311) surfaces, respectively.

The dehydrogenation step was modeled using the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) approach, where the chemical potential of H+ + e- is referenced to 0.5H 43. This method avoids explicitly modeling H adsorption sites. The Gibbs free energy was corrected by including zero-point energy and entropy contributions obtained from vibrational frequency calculations.

## Paper

## Abstract

The manufacture of nitriles is critical to various industrial applications, but poor selectivity results in the significant release of pollutive byproducts such as CO , NO and toxic cyanide. Here, we report the electrochemical conversion of benzaldehyde to benzonitrile at near-unity selectivity, during which Co O clusters-decorated Cu O electrocatalyst activates the C−N bond of an unstable intermediate species. Operando spectroelectrochemical studies and theoretical calculations reveal that benzaldehyde couples with NH to form the phenylmethanimine intermediate bound atop Cu2+ active sites, which facilitates hydrogen transfer from the imine group to nearby surface oxygen. Our electrochemical system can convert aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes to the corresponding nitriles at Faradaic efficiencies of 78-97%. This can be paired with cathodic NO reduction, which produces a commensurable amount of NH to that consumed even at a current density of 200 mA cm-2. Our work offers a clean synthetic route to otherwise-pollutive chemicals, and also expands the repertoire of organonitrogen compounds that can be accessed by electrocatalysis.

---

## Introduction

Nitriles have far-ranging applications in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, dyes and polymers1. For example, benzonitrile is manufactured at 10 million kg per year due to its importance as a building block in pharmaceuticals and melamine resins2. Currently, nitriles are manufactured through the ammoxidation of alkanes3,4, alcohols or aldehydes5 with ammonia and oxygen at high temperatures (Fig. 1a). These conditions require heavy energy consumption and result in low selectivity, leading to the release of CO , NO and over-oxidation products6. Other synthesis methods, such as the Sandmeyer reaction and Rosenmund-von Braun reaction, require stoichiometric amounts of toxic cyanide reagents7,8 (Fig. 1b); more than one million tons of cyanide are consumed per year by the chemicals industry9, which generate hazardous wastes due to incomplete cyanide consumption or production of cyanide derivatives10. Thus, it is important to develop cleaner methods of nitriles synthesis that can utilize renewable energy and benign conditions, while avoiding cyanide reagents.

Recently, there has been great interest in electrochemical C−N coupling reactions, as they offer a sustainable route for producing valuable organonitrogen compounds such as urea, amides, amines, oximes and amino acids11-25. Comparatively, nitriles have a higher degree of unsaturation; a different electrochemical route must be designed to access this type of C≡N bond. Previously, it has been reported that copper salt can catalyze the thermal ammoxidation of aldehydes to nitriles; Cu2+ binds to the aldimine intermediate to form an iminylcuprate complex, which then dissociates to Cu+ and the nitrile product26. This led us to consider the possibility of enabling ‘electrochemical ammoxidation’ by building Cuδ+ into our electrocatalyst. We also note that the oxidative nature of the reaction means that it can be coupled to the cathodic nitrogen oxides reduction reaction (NO RR) to NH , which suggests that waste NO in industrial exhaust can be utilized as a N-source to enhance the sustainability of the reaction (Fig. 1c).

In this work, we demonstrate the electrocatalytic conversion of benzaldehyde to benzonitrile using NH as a benign nitrogen source under ambient conditions. This is achieved with an electrocatalyst comprising Co O clusters-decorated Cu O nanorod array (Co OS/Cu O), which enabled Faradaic efficiency of 98.7(±1.1)% and near-unity selectivity under an applied potential of 1.35 V vs. RHE. The electrocatalyst remains stable with Faradaic efficiency averaging 95.4(±2.5)% over 100 hours. Operando spectroelectrochemical and density function theory (DFT) studies show that benzaldehyde couples with NH to form an unstable phenylmethanimine intermediate, which subsequently undergoes Cuδ+-mediated electrochemical dehydrogenation to benzonitrile. The electrochemical benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion can be integrated into reaction pathways that enable the nitrilation of more challenging alcohol and alkyl groups. Our electrochemical system can also convert other aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes, including those derived from CO , to the corresponding nitriles with Faradaic efficiencies of 78-97%. Finally, we demonstrated tandem benzonitrile electrosynthesis and NO RR at current densities up to 200 mA cm-2.

---

## Results

Electrocatalyst design and characterization
We prepared the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst by chemical oxidation of copper foam in an aqueous NaOH and (NH ) S O solution, which embellished the surface with Cu(OH) nanorods, followed by immersion in a solution containing ZIF-67 metal-organic framework and annealing in air at 350°C (see characterization of the Cu(OH) and ZIF-67/Cu(OH) nanorod arrays in Supplementary Figs. 1-2). Co K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy indicated that the ZIF-67 was successfully converted to Co O , as the absorption edge of Co O /Cu O displayed identical features to that of the Co O standard (Supplementary Fig. 3). The Fourier-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra revealed oscillations corresponding to Co−O, the Co−Co bond with octahedral centers, and the Co−Co bond with octahedral and tetrahedral centers, which further confirms the formation of Co O cluster27. High-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) with corresponding EDX mapping showed that the Co O cluster took the form of a slightly concave octahedron attached to the tip of the Cu O nanorod (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 4). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed an array of cluster-on-nanorod morphology on the copper foam surface (Fig. 2b). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern showed peaks at 35.5°, 38.7°, 61.5° corresponding to (11-1), (111) and (11-3) lattice planes of CuO, as well as 36.5° and 61.5° corresponding to (111) and (220) lattice planes of Cu O (Supplementary Fig. 5)28. This is corroborated by high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), which revealed crystalline phases with lattice spacings of 0.242 and 0.234 nm corresponding to Cu O(111) and CuO(111), respectively. It should be noted that both Cu O(110) and Cu O(111) facets were observed (Supplementary Fig. 6), with the dominant one being the (111) surface. The Co O cluster also appeared to be highly crystalline, with lattice spacings of 0.246 and 0.287 nm corresponding to (311) and (220) planes (Fig. 2c).

Electrochemical conversion of benzaldehyde to benzonitrile
The electrochemical C−N coupling of benzaldehyde and ammonia to benzonitrile was conducted in a three-electrode H-type cell, with a working electrode comprising Co O /Cu O on copper foam, an Ag/AgCl reference electrode and a platinum plate counter electrode (Supplementary Fig. 7). The optimal anolyte concentration comprised 0.04 M benzaldehyde, 2.0 M NH and 0.1 M NaOH in a 41:9 water:acetonitrile mixture (Supplementary Fig. 8-9). The catholyte is an aqueous 0.1 M NaOH solution, and is separated from the anolyte by Nafion® 117 membrane. The Faradaic efficiencies towards benzonitrile showed a volcano-type tendency in the potential range of 1.15-1.65 V vs. RHE, with the optimal Faradaic efficiency at 98.7(±1.1)% at 1.35 V vs. RHE (Fig. 2d). Beyond 1.55 V vs. RHE, the Faradaic efficiency decreases significantly due to competing NH oxidation reaction. This is corroborated by the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curve, which revealed the NH oxidation peak to be about 1.5 V vs. RHE under reaction conditions (Supplementary Fig. 10). The yield of benzonitrile reached 48.6(±6.7)% after 1 hour of reaction at 1.55 V vs. RHE, and further increased to 75.0(±1.5)% after 3 hours (Supplementary Fig. 11). The selectivity towards benzonitrile was ~100% with no obvious byproducts detected (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Figs. 12-13). No benzonitrile was detected at open-circuit voltage (OCV), without applied potential or in the absence of NH , which confirms the electrochemical nature of the reaction and the important role of NH as the nitrogen source (Supplementary Fig. 14).

We investigated the robustness of the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst by subjecting it to a constant potential of 1.35 V vs. RHE for 100 hours, during which portions of the electrolyte were periodically removed for analysis and replaced with fresh electrolyte. Under these conditions, the electrocatalyst achieved a stable current density of ~10 mA cm-2, with an average Faradaic efficiency of 95.4(±2.5)% (Fig. 2e). Post-reaction characterizations of the electrocatalyst (i.e., SEM, EDX, XANES, EXAFS and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), see Supplementary Figs. 15-18) showed no obvious change in the structure or composition, which suggests its compatibility for long-term operation.

Investigation of reaction mechanism
Having established the efficacy of Co O /Cu O towards benzonitrile production, we studied the role of different components in the electrocatalyst. The Cu O electrocatalyst without Co O clusters was also prepared (see characterization in Supplementary Figs. 19-20) and yielded a Faradaic efficiency of 71.8(±3.1)% at 1.35 V vs. RHE, which suggests that Cu O functions as the main catalytic component driving the benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion (Supplementary Fig. 21). Only trace benzonitrile product was detected when pristine copper foam (CF) was used as the working electrode (Supplementary Fig. 22), which suggests that either Cu2+ or Cu+ should function as the electrocatalytic active site in Cu O. We performed operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to study the electrode/electrolyte interface during reaction (Fig. 3a)29. At potentials between 0.5-1.0 V vs. RHE, we observed a signal in the middle-frequency region (100-102 Hz) that corresponds to the electrooxidation of the Cu O catalyst (i.e., Cu0Cu+Cu2+). This is consistent with the cyclic voltammetry (CV) curve, which showed two distinct oxidation peaks at 0.60 and 0.85 V vs. RHE corresponding to Cu0Cu+ and Cu0/Cu+Cu2+, respectively28 (Supplementary Fig. 23). At potentials >1.05 V vs. RHE, the signal is observed in the low-frequency region (10-1-100 Hz), which is related to the appearance of oxidation species on the surface of the electrode. This signifies that the structural evolution of Cuδ+ is complete and the benzaldehyde electrosynthesis occurs. In situ Raman spectroscopy showed distinctive peaks at 218 and 294 cm−1 at OCV, which can be attributed to Cu O and CuO, respectively (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Figs. 24-25). In the absence of benzaldehyde and NH , the Cu O peak disappeared at 1.35 V vs. RHE, indicating the oxidation of Cu+ to Cu2+. With benzaldehyde and NH , the Cu O peak can still be observed at 1.35 V vs. RHE, while the CuO peak showed reduced intensity compared to that at OCV, which suggests that Cu2+ catalyzed the benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion and was reverted to Cu+ in the process.

The reaction mechanism was further probed using in situ attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), by tracking the adsorbed intermediates and products on Cu O/CF at potentials from OCV to 1.65 V vs. RHE (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 26). Under OCV, peaks were observed at 1700, 1371, 1233 and 1138 cm-1, which could be assigned to the C=O stretching vibration of benzaldehyde, alcoholic O−H group, the N−H twisting vibration of CH −NH structure and the NH stretching vibration of CH −NH structure, respectively23,30. This implies that NH , which has a relatively strong nucleophilicity, can spontaneously attack benzaldehyde to form amino(phenyl)methanol, which undergoes dehydration to generate the unstable *benzyl-azane intermediate. As the potential increased to 1.15 V vs. RHE, the NH peak at 1138 cm-1 is diminished while the N−H peak at 1233 cm-1 is slightly enhanced. We observed the emergence of peaks corresponding to the N−H stretching vibration of CH=NH structure at 1296 cm-1, C=N stretching vibration at 1624 cm-1 and C≡N stretching vibration at 2259 cm-1, which indicates the formation of phenylmethanimine intermediate and benzonitrile product23,30. As the potential increases up to 1.65 V vs. RHE, the NH and N−H absorption peaks of unstable amino(phenyl)methanol and *benzyl-azane intermediates are weakened, whereas the C=N bond and C≡N peaks of phenylmethanimine and benzonitrile are generally strengthened. This signified that amino(phenyl)methanol and *benzyl-azane intermediates rapidly converted to the critical phenylmethanimine intermediate, which subsequently could be dehydrogenated to generate the benzonitrile. Liquid chromatography-quadrupole time of flight mass spectrometry (LC-QTOF) also ascertained the presence of phenylmethanimine intermediate and benzonitrile product in the post-reaction anolyte (Fig. 3d). The use of 15N-labelled NH yielded 15N-labelled phenylmethanimine and benzonitrile, which reinforced the important role of NH as a nitrogen source in benzonitrile electrosynthesis (Supplementary Fig. 27). Taken together, we postulate that NH readily undergoes C−N coupling with the carbonyl group of benzaldehyde to form an unstable phenylmethanimine intermediate, which subsequently undergoes Cuδ+-mediated electrochemical dehydrogenation to yield the benzonitrile product (Fig. 3e).

We further investigated the Cuδ+-mediated dehydrogenation step through density functional theory (DFT) calculations. A CuO(111) slab model with four atomic layers was constructed, upon which several initial adsorption geometries were examined. The most stable configuration features the imine nitrogen of phenylmethanimine (Ph−CH=NH) binding to a single two-coordinate Cu atom (Configuration 1 in Supplementary Fig. 28). This geometry suggests a possible adsorption mode in which the =NH moiety is in proximity with the surface, potentially enabling the abstraction of the N-bound hydrogen. Within the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) framework, this hydrogen is removed as a coupled proton–electron pair rather than transferred to or stabilized on any surface atoms31. The resultant molecule adopts an sp3-like configuration and relocates to a bridge site coordinated by two Cu atoms (Supplementary Figs. 29c,d). The hydrogen atom from the CH= moiety is then abstracted by the surface to form the nitrile product (C≡N), culminating in the final state where the nitrogen atom bind s atop a single Cu atom (Supplementary Figs. 29e,f). This second hydrogen transfer is calculated to be thermodynamically more favorable than the first, as reflected by the downhill reaction energy (G). Overall, the G of phenylmethanimine dehydrogenation on CuO(111) is 0.70 eV (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Table 2). In contrast, phenylmethanimine dehydrogenation on Cu O(110) has a higher G of 1.16 eV (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Figs. 30-31), suggesting that Cu2+ species may be more effective for phenylmethanimine dehydrogenation than Cu+ species under the modeled conditions. This is substantiated by Bader charge analysis of the adsorbed phenylmethanimine on CuO(111). As reaction progresses, the phenylmethanimine molecular fragment exhibits an increasingly positive charge; from +0.16 in the initial adsorbed state to +0.85 in the first dehydrogenated intermediate and +2.10 in the final nitrile product (Supplementary Table 3). Correspondingly, CuO(111) exhibits increasingly negative charge (−0.16 → −0.85 → −2.10), which is indicative that the surface Cu2⁺ accepts electrons from phenylmethanimine and is reduced to Cu⁺.

To elucidate the influence of the Co O cluster, we similarly examined the phenylmethanimine dehydrogenation step on the Co O (311) surface (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Figs. 32-33). The calculated G of 0.96 eV lies between those of CuO(111) and Cu O(111), indicating an intermediate oxidizing strength within this computational model. It should be noted that these DFT results are based on idealized static slab models and mainly provide qualitative trends under real catalytic conditions. Experimentally, the Faradaic efficiency of benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion using Co O clusters supported on carbon paper is 32.6(±3.8)% (Supplementary Fig. 34), which suggests that the Co O clusters provide additional active sites that contribute to the enhanced Faradaic efficiency of Co O /Cu O. This is corroborated by the increased double-layer capacitance (C ) of Co O /Cu O compared to Cu O (2.06 versus 1.70 mF cm−2, see Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 35). We also investigated the electronic structure of Co O /Cu O through XPS analysis (Fig. 4b-4c and Supplementary Figs. 36-37). High-resolution Co 2p XPS spectrum showed a negative shift compared to that of pure Co O powder, signifying a lower average Co oxidation state. Cu 2p XPS spectrum of Co O /Cu O showed a higher energy shift compared to that of Cu O, which indicates a higher average Cu oxidation state and suggests electron transfer from Cu to Co within the Co O /Cu O material. The higher average Cu oxidation state promotes the Cuδ+-mediated dehydrogenation step, thereby enabling higher Faradaic efficiencies for electrochemical benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversion (Supplementary Fig. 34). Therefore, the decoration of Co O clusters on Cu O electrocatalyst not only increases the active sites, but can potentially modulate the electronic structure of the electrocatalyst, resulting in a higher average Cu oxidation state promoting the Cuδ+-mediated dehydrogenation step.

Electrosynthesis of various nitriles and utilization of NO
The broad applicability of Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst was demonstrated through the electrochemical conversion of various aldehydes to the corresponding nitriles at near-unity selectivities (Supplementary Fig. 38). An application scenario is the electrosynthesis of 2,6-dichlorobenzonitrile, an important herbicide with a market size of $23 million per year32,33; we achieved Faradaic efficiency of 81.2(±1.7)% at 1.35 V vs. RHE. The presence of electron-withdrawing groups such as −Cl, −Br and −CN generally led to higher Faradaic efficiencies of 93-97%, as the enhanced electrophilicity of these benzaldehydes promotes C−N coupling with nucleophilic NH . For electron-donating −CH and −OCH groups, Faradaic efficiencies were lower at 84.2(±6.1) and 77.8(±2.5)%. The Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst can be extended to the electrosynthesis of aliphatic nitriles, such as acetonitrile with a Faradaic efficiency of 86.2(±4.7)%. It should be noted that the acetaldehyde precursor can be obtained from electrochemical CO reduction reaction, thereby enabling the electrosynthesis of nitriles from renewable sources34. We also demonstrated that nitrile electrosynthesis can be integrated into reaction pathways starting from precursors with alcohol and even alkyl groups (Fig. 4d). For example, the electrochemical benzyl alcohol-to-benzonitrile conversion can be achieved Faradaic efficiency at 43.1(±2.0)% (Supplementary Fig. 39). The electrochemical toluene-to-benzonitrile conversion was conducted in two stages; toluene was first oxidized at 100 mA cm-2 for 2 h using a CoO /IrO on Ti mesh electrode to activate the C(sp3)−H bond and achieve sufficient benzaldehyde intermediate, after which NH was added and the reaction continued at 25 mA cm-2 to enable benzonitrile using the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst (Supplementary Fig. 40).

Finally, we considered that the electrochemical valorization of waste NO to nitrogenous chemicals can mitigate pollution and reduce dependence on valuable NH as a nitrogen source. We therefore coupled cathodic NO RR with anodic benzonitrile electrosynthesis in a single electrochemical cell, with the former acting as a NH supply for the latter. The cathode was oxide-derived Cu (OD-Cu) synthesized by electrochemically reducing Cu O (Supplementary Fig. 41), and the catholyte comprised 0.1 M KNO in 1 M NaOH. As NH in the anolyte can crossover the Nafion membrane and lead to a higher-than-actual NO RR Faradaic efficiency, we employed a decoupled electrolyzer connected by O /H O redox couple, which can better separate the catholyte and anolyte in order to accurately quantify the amount of NH produced at the cathode (Supplementary Fig. 42). Notably, the NH consumption at anode was comparable to NH production at cathode even at current densities up to 200 mA cm-2, which signifies that waste NO can be viably incorporated into valuable nitriles (Figure 4e, Faradaic efficiencies can be found in Supplementary Fig. 43). This also means that the achieved partial current densities and production rates are competitive with other reported nitrile electrosynthesis, while maintaining near-unity selectivity (Supplementary Table 4).

Synthesis and characterization of the Co O /Cu O nanorod array electrocatalyst
The Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst was synthesized by the modified chemical oxidation followed by annealing procedure. Cu foam was ultrasonically cleaned in 3 M HCl solution for 10 min, then in a mixture of acetone and deionized water for another 10 min. The pretreated Cu foam was soaked into a 40 mL aqueous solution containing 4 g NaOH and 1.5 g (NH ) S O for 1 h, then washed with deionized water and ethanol. The resultant Cu(OH) nanorod array was prepared after drying at 60°C. Cu(OH) was immersed into 2 mmol cobaltous nitrate hexahydrate in methanol solution for 10 min, after which 8 mmol 2-methylimidazole in methanol solution was added under stirring and allowed to stand for 6 h. The resultant ZIF-67/Cu(OH) was taken out, washed with deionized water and methanol, dried at 60°C, then annealed at 350°C for 3 h, 2°C min-1 to form the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst.

Electrocatalyst characterization
To characterize the Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst, X-ray diffraction (XRD) was detected on Bruker® D8 ADVANCE with Cu Kα source. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were obtained on a Hitachi SU8220 FESEM at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. Energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy was collected with an on-board AMTEK® Octane Elite EDS System, with an accelerating voltage of 20 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were obtained on TEM JEOL 2100F. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was measured on a PHI Quantum 2000 XPS system. X-Ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) was conducted on XAFCA beamline at the Singapore Synchrotron Light Source (SSLS).

Evaluation of electrochemical performance
The electrochemical benzaldehyde-to-benzonitrile conversions were conducted in H-type electrolytic cell (purchased from Tianjin Aida). The electrolyte was prepared individually before each experimental run. The anolyte comprised 0.04 M benzaldehyde, 2.0 M NH and 0.1 M NaOH in 41:9 water:acetonitrile mixture (pH=13.16(±0.07)). The catholyte was 0.1 M aqueous NaOH catholyte. The overall reactor configuration comprised 15 mL of anolyte and 15 mL of catholyte, separated by Nafion® 117 membrane (size 2.5 cm by 2.5 cm, thickness 0.18mm). The Nafion® 117 membrane was activated in 0.5 M H SO solution at 80°C for 2 hours and stored in MilliQ water (18.2 MΩ). The working electrode was Co O /Cu O electrocatalyst on copper foam (1×1 cm2), the counter electrode was a platinum plate, and the reference was an Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) electrode. Unless otherwise stated, the duration of the electrochemical reaction is 1 hour. All electrochemical measurements were performed using the Metrohm Autolab potentiostat PGSTAT204 without iR correction. All the potentials were provided without iR corrected and converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) with the following equation:
E = E + 0.0591 × pH + 0.197 (1)
RHE Ag/AgCl

The cyclic voltammetry (CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves were measured at a scan rate of 5 mV s-1. In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were tested at the potentials of 0.45 to 1.65 V vs. RHE with a frequency range from 10−1 to 105 Hz with an alternating-current amplitude of 10 mV. Electrochemical double-layer capacitance (C ) measurement was carried out by CV method with different scan rates in the non-Faradaic region. The C value was obtained from the slopes of the current density–scan rate plots. The 100-hour stability test was conducted at 1.35 V vs. RHE, during which portions of the electrolyte were periodically removed for analysis and replaced with fresh electrolyte. In universality tests and the integrated electrosynthesis system starting from other precursors, different precursors were added to the anolyte using a similar electrolysis procedure.

The qualitative and quantitative analysis of the products produced in anolyte was determined using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, Agilent 1260) equipped with a DAD detector and an Eclipse Plus C18 column (4.6×150 mm). The mobile phase is ultrapure water/acetonitrile (v/v = 70% : 30%) with a flow rate of 1.0 ml min-1 and column temperature of 25°C. The formation of products in anolyte was further ensured by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, Bruker AV400SB) with water suppression and liquid chromatography-quadrupole time of flight mass spectrometry (LC-QTOF, Agilent 6545) with 90% ultrapure water and 10% acetonitrile as flowing eluent.

The Faradaic efficiency, reaction rate, selectivity, conversion and yield for liquid product are calculated using the following equations:
Faradaic efficiency (%) = (N × F × C × V) / Q × 100% (2)
Reaction rate (μmol cm-1 h-1) = (C × V) / (S × t) (3)
Selectivity (%) = (C × V) / n × 100% (4)
Conversion (%) = n / n × 100% (5)
Yield (%) = Conversion × Selectivity (6)
where N is the number of electron transfer to generated product, F is the Faraday constant (96485 C mol−1), C is the concentration of liquid products after the electrosynthesis reaction, V is the volume of the electrolyte, Q is the total charge during the electrosynthesis process, S is the electrode area, t is the electrolysis time, n is the mole amount of consumed feedstock, n is the mole amount of initial feedstock.

Operando spectroelectrochemical studies
In situ ATR-SEIRAS was conducted using PerkinElmer Frontier FT-IR spectrometer equipped with a mercury cadmium telluride (MCT) detector. The measurements were carried out in a commercial electrochemical cell containing benzaldehyde and NH in 0.1 M aqueous NaOH electrolyte. The electrode was Cu O electrocatalyst on an Au film chemically deposited on the reflecting plane of the ATR Si prism. The background spectrum without applied potential was acquired at electrolyte condition before each systemic measurement. In situ spectra were collected under potentials of OCV and 1.15-1.65 V vs. RHE, by averaging 50 scans with a resolution of 4 cm-1 and subtracting the infrared background.

In situ Raman spectra were recorded using a Horiba LabRam Odyssey Nano Raman Spectrometer system with 633 nm laser. The Raman cell was equipped with a working electrode comprising Cu O deposited on carbon paper, an Ag/AgCl reference electrode and a Pt wire counter electrode. The cell was filled with benzaldehyde and NH in 0.1 M NaOH electrolyte. An Olympus N2667700 water immersion objective was submerged in the electrolyte to collect in situ Raman spectra under different electrochemical conditions.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations
All periodic slab calculations were carried out using density functional theory (DFT) as implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)35. The Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE)36 exchange-correlation functional within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) was employed, along with projector-augmented wave (PAW)37 potentials and a plane-wave energy cutoff of 500 eV. Dispersion interactions were accounted for using the DFT-D3 method38.

Slab models of CuO(111) and Cu O(111) and Co O (311) surfaces were constructed with four atomic layers, where the bottom three layers were fixed during structural optimizations. The CuO(111) slab has lattice parameters a = 17.30 Å, b = 18.95 Å, and c = 28.26 Å, with interaxial angles α = β = 90° and γ = 107.76°. The Cu O(111) surface adopts a = 18.12 Å, b = 18.12 Å, and c = 31.10 Å, with α = β = 90° and γ = 120.00°. The Co O (311) slab exhibits a = 19.85 Å, b = 22.93 Å, and c = 26.31 Å, with α = β = 90° and γ = 106.78°. In all models, the c-axis is oriented normal to the surface plane, and a vacuum region of approximately 20 Å was added along this direction to prevent spurious interactions between periodic images. Brillouin zone sampling was performed using a Γ-centered 1 × 1 × 1 k-point mesh for all adsorption geometry optimizations39. Structural relaxations were conducted until the forces on each atom were below 0.02 eV/Å and the total energy change between successive steps was less than 10-5 eV. To account for the on-site Coulomb interactions in the localized 3d orbitals, the DFT+U method40 was applied with U = 7.0 eV for Cu in CuO41 and U = 4.0 eV for Co in Co O 42.

To rigorously assess the influence of k-point sampling for slabs of this size, we performed a convergence test on the Cu O model (Supplementary Table 1). Increasing the k-point mesh from 1×1×1 to 2×2×1 resulted in only marginal variations (≤0.01 eV) in the computed energy profiles, thereby confirming that Γ-point sampling is sufficient for this lateral cell dimension. On this basis, and given the nearly identical cell sizes across all three systems, the Γ-point (1×1×1) mesh validated for Cu O was consistently used for the CuO and Co O slabs in all subsequent calculations.

For all surfaces, only coordinatively unsaturated (CUS) metal sites were considered as potential adsorption sites. Guided by the surface symmetry and the locations of coordinatively unsaturated sites, we evaluated three, two, and three distinct adsorption geometries on the CuO(111), Cu O(111) and Co O (311) surfaces, respectively.

The dehydrogenation step was modeled using the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) approach, where the chemical potential of H+ + e- is referenced to 0.5H 43. This method avoids explicitly modeling H adsorption sites. The Gibbs free energy was corrected by including zero-point energy and entropy contributions obtained from vibrational frequency calculations.
